title: Chrome 155 Update for Google Book: Expanded Web App Installs & Seamless Integration Unveiled
body:
Google has rolled out Chrome 155 for its Chrome OS‑based “Googlebook” devices, a move that widens the scope for Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) and deepens their integration with the operating system. The update lets users install web‑based applications more broadly across the device, granting them native‑like permissions, background operation, and tighter ties to system services such as notifications, file handling, and multi‑window support. By blurring the line between traditional desktop software and browser‑delivered experiences, Chrome 155 signals Google’s intent to make its hybrid laptops a more compelling platform for developers and enterprise users alike.

The most noticeable change is the removal of previous restrictions that limited web‑app installations to a narrow set of use cases. Under Chrome 155, any PWA that meets the new manifest criteria can be added to the device’s app drawer, appear in the launcher, and be managed through the same settings panel used for native applications. This includes the ability to run in the background, receive push notifications, and interact with the file system without prompting the user each time. For power users, the update also introduces support for “installable shortcuts,” allowing a single web link to behave like a full‑fledged app with its own icon, splash screen, and offline caching.

Developers stand to benefit from a more streamlined path to distribution. Google has expanded the Chrome Web Store’s verification process, offering a “Trusted Web Activity” (TWA) badge for PWAs that meet performance, security, and accessibility standards. Apps that earn the badge gain access to additional APIs, such as the new “system‑wide clipboard” and “media session” controls, which were previously reserved for native code. This encourages developers to invest in web‑first strategies, reducing the need to maintain separate codebases for Android, Chrome OS, and other desktop platforms. Early adopters, including productivity suites and media streaming services, have already reported smoother onboarding and higher retention rates on Googlebooks.

From a market perspective, the upgrade aligns with Google’s broader push to position Chrome OS as a viable alternative to Windows and macOS in the education and enterprise sectors. By enhancing PWA capabilities, the company addresses a long‑standing criticism that Chrome OS devices rely too heavily on web browsers and lack the depth of native software ecosystems. Schools that deploy Googlebooks for classroom use can now offer students a richer set of tools—such as offline‑capable note‑taking apps and collaborative editors—without the overhead of managing multiple installations. Likewise, businesses can leverage the tighter integration to roll out custom internal tools that behave like traditional desktop applications while remaining easy to update centrally.

Security considerations have also been front‑and‑center in the rollout. Chrome 155 introduces stricter sandboxing for installed PWAs, ensuring that each app runs in an isolated process with limited access to system resources. The update mandates HTTPS‑only delivery for installable web apps, and adds a new “permission‑audit” dashboard where users can review and revoke privileges granted to PWAs. These measures aim to mitigate the risk of malicious web content masquerading as legitimate software—a concern that has shadowed the growth of PWAs since their inception.

Looking ahead, the expanded PWA support on Googlebooks could set a precedent for other operating systems to embrace web‑first applications more fully. As developers increasingly prioritize cross‑platform compatibility, the line between native and web experiences may continue to dissolve, prompting hardware manufacturers to rethink the balance of pre‑installed software versus cloud‑delivered services. For Google, the success of Chrome 155 will likely be measured by adoption rates among educational institutions and enterprise fleets, as well as the volume of high‑quality PWAs that emerge in the Chrome Web Store. If the update delivers on its promise of seamless integration and robust security, it could accelerate Chrome OS’s evolution from a niche browser‑centric platform to a mainstream desktop contender.
